description.en: The alternate toe tap leg lift is a low impact ab exercise that alternates lowering each leg to tap the floor. The slow controlled tap challenges the lower abs to resist anterior pelvic tilt.

en: Lie flat on your back with both legs straight up toward the ceiling.
Place your hands at your sides or under your hips for support.
Brace the core and press the lower back into the floor.
Slowly lower one leg toward the floor while keeping it straight.
Lightly tap the heel to the floor without losing core engagement.
Lift the leg back to vertical with control.
Repeat with the opposite leg.
Continue alternating taps for the full set.
Builds lower abdominal strength and control.
Trains the hip flexors with strict eccentrics.
Improves lumbo pelvic stability.
Joint friendly and beginner accessible.
No equipment needed.
Excellent core warm up before lifting.

description.en: The assisted pull-up uses a counterweight pull-up machine that offsets part of your bodyweight, allowing you to perform pull-ups with proper form even if you cannot do unassisted reps. It is the most popular machine-based pull-up progression and is available in most commercial gyms.

en: Set the counterweight on the machine. Higher weight means more assistance — start heavier and reduce over time.
Grip the wide pull-up handles with an overhand grip.
Kneel or stand on the assistance pad.
Pull yourself up by driving your elbows down and back until your chin clears the bar.
Squeeze your lats at the top.
Lower under control over two to three seconds.
Reduce the counterweight by 5 to 10 lbs as you get stronger.
Goal: work toward zero assistance and unassisted pull-ups.
Develops pull-up strength progressively
Adjustable assistance for all fitness levels
Safe and controlled
Available in most commercial gyms
Builds pulling strength toward unassisted pull-ups
Excellent for beginners

description.en: The band lying hip internal rotation is a hip rotator drill that uses a resistance band looped around the feet. The mover lies on one side and rotates the top foot inward against band tension. It builds hip internal rotation strength.

en: Loop a resistance band around both feet.
Lie on one side with the knees bent at ninety degrees.
Stack the hips and shoulders.
Brace your core and keep the knees together.
Rotate the top foot inward toward the floor.
Hold the rotation against the band tension.
Return with control to the start.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Trains hip internal rotation
Builds hip stability
Strong rotator move
Useful warm-up
Builds the glutes

description.en: The bar band squat attaches resistance bands from the floor or rack to the ends of the barbell during a back squat. The bands provide accommodating resistance, increasing tension as you stand up. It overloads the lockout where the legs are strongest and is a powerlifting staple for breaking plateaus.

en: Attach resistance bands from the floor anchors to the ends of the barbell.
Step under the bar and place it across your upper traps.
Take a shoulder-width stance with toes pointed slightly out.
Brace your core and pull the bar tight onto your back.
Squat down by sitting your hips back and bending the knees.
Continue until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor.
Drive up through your heels against the band tension.
Lock out at the top with hips fully extended.
Accommodating resistance overloads the top
Builds explosive squat power
Useful for breaking plateaus
Powerlifting staple
Trains hip and knee extension speed
Strong leg builder

description.en: The barbell high bar squat is the Olympic weightlifting style of squatting where the barbell rests high on the upper trapezius, just below the base of the neck. The high bar position requires a more upright torso and emphasizes the quadriceps more than the low bar position. It is the squat of choice for Olympic lifters.

en: Set a barbell at upper-chest height in a power rack.
Step under the bar and place it across your upper traps, just below the base of your neck.
Grip the bar shoulder-width or slightly wider. Pull your elbows down and back.
Unrack and step back into squat stance — feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned out slightly.
Brace your core hard. Maintain an upright torso.
Sit straight down, keeping your torso vertical and chest tall.
Descend until your hip crease drops below your knees.
Drive through your full foot to stand. Repeat for the desired reps.
Emphasizes the quadriceps more than low bar squat
Allows deeper squat depth
Translates to Olympic lifting
Builds quad and glute size
Improves squat mobility
Standard squat in CrossFit and Olympic lifting

description.en: The barbell power shrug combines an explosive trap shrug with a small dip and drive from the legs. The leg drive allows you to use much heavier weight than a strict shrug, creating massive trap overload. It is essentially a high-pull without the pulling phase, used in Olympic lifting prep and trap development.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold a heavy barbell in front of your thighs with an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Brace your core. Pull your shoulders back and down.
Dip slightly by bending your knees about 4 inches. Keep torso upright.
Reverse the dip explosively — drive through your feet and explode upward.
As you stand explosively, shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears with maximum force.
The leg drive contributes to the force, allowing heavier loads.
Lower the bar under control back to the start.
Use heavy weight. Aim for 5 to 8 explosive reps per set.
Allows much heavier loading than strict shrugs
Builds massive trap thickness
Develops explosive power
Useful for Olympic lifting prep
Trains rate of force development
Time-efficient trap exercise

description.en: The barbell single-leg deadlift is a unilateral hip-hinge exercise where you balance on one leg and hinge to lower a loaded barbell toward the floor. The barbell version allows much heavier loading than the dumbbell or kettlebell version, building serious posterior-chain strength on each side independently. It is a demanding exercise that requires strong balance and core control — best for intermediate-to-advanced lifters.

en: Set a loaded barbell on the floor in front of you. Stand tall just behind the bar with feet hip-width apart.
Lift one foot slightly off the floor (your “back” leg). Soft-bend your standing knee and lock that angle in.
Brace your core hard and pull your shoulders back.
Hinge forward at the standing hip while letting your back leg lift behind you to counterbalance. Reach down with both hands to grip the bar.
Set your back flat. Keep your hips square — do not let the lifted-leg hip rotate up.
Drive your standing foot through the floor and pull the bar up by extending your standing hip. Stand fully tall while keeping the back leg lifted.
Lower the bar back down by hinging at the hip and lifting the back leg behind you. Touch the bar to the floor under control.
Complete all reps on the standing leg, then switch sides. Use lighter weight than your conventional deadlift — this lift is much harder than it looks.
Allows heavier loading than dumbbell or kettlebell single-leg deadlifts
Builds the glutes and hamstrings unilaterally
Trains balance, ankle stability, and core control under heavy load
Exposes and corrects left-right strength imbalances
Carries over to athletic performance and injury prevention
Excellent accessory for the conventional deadlift

description.en: The body-up starts in a forearm plank and presses up to a high plank by extending both arms simultaneously (unlike commando planks which alternate). It is a demanding tricep and shoulder exercise because both arms press at once.

en: Start in a forearm plank. Body straight, core braced.
Press both hands into the floor simultaneously to push up to a high plank.
Both arms extend at the same time — unlike alternating commando planks.
Lower both forearms back to the floor simultaneously.
Continue pressing up and lowering for reps.
This requires significant tricep and shoulder strength.
Maintain body alignment throughout.
Aim for 5 to 10 reps.
Simultaneous arm press builds tricep power
Harder than alternating commando planks
Develops explosive pressing from forearms
No equipment needed
Builds tricep and shoulder strength
Advanced plank variation

description.en: The bodyweight glute dominant step up tweaks the standard step up by leaning the torso forward to bias the glutes. The forward lean keeps the hamstrings and glutes loaded throughout the rep.

en: Stand facing a sturdy box or bench at about knee height.
Place one foot flat on top of the box.
Lean the torso forward at the hips with a flat back.
Brace the core and shift your weight onto the front foot.
Drive through the heel of the front foot to step up onto the box.
Maintain the forward torso lean throughout the step up.
Step back down with control, keeping the lean.
Complete all reps on one side then switch legs.
Hits the glutes harder than a standard step up.
Builds single leg strength and balance.
Forward lean reduces quad dominance.
No equipment beyond a box or bench.
Trains the hamstrings through hip extension.
Excellent at home glute builder.

description.en: The bodyweight standing around the world with wall support traces a full circle around the body with one arm against the wall. The wall keeps the arm path honest as the shoulder moves through a full circumduction.

en: Stand sideways to a wall with one shoulder close to it.
Place the inside hand on the wall at hip height.
Brace the core and keep the shoulder relaxed.
Slide the hand up the wall toward the ceiling.
Continue tracing the arm overhead and back behind you.
Bring the hand all the way down behind your hip.
Reverse the motion to come back to the start.
Repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Mobilizes the shoulder through a full circle.
Wall feedback keeps the shoulder blade tracking honestly.
No equipment needed beyond a wall.
Excellent warm up for overhead lifts.
Improves shoulder mobility.
Reduces shoulder stiffness.

description.en: The bodyweight standing scapula row is a postural drill that mimics the pulling motion of a row while standing tall. The arms move back as the shoulder blades retract to train scapular control. It is excellent as a posture drill and an upper back warm-up.

en: Stand tall with feet at hip-width and arms extended out in front.
Make loose fists with palms facing each other.
Brace your core and keep your chest tall.
Pull your elbows back as if rowing a bar.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together and down.
Stop with the elbows just past your sides.
Hold the squeeze briefly at the back position.
Return to the start and repeat with smooth tempo.
Trains scapular retraction
Useful posture drill
No equipment needed
Excellent warm-up move
Builds upper back control
Easy to add to any session

description.en: The bottle weighted glute bridge is a weighted glute bridge using a water bottle for at-home loading. The lifter lies on the back with a bottle held across the hips and drives the hips up. The added load makes the glute squeeze stronger than bodyweight.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Place a filled water bottle across the hips.
Hold the bottle in place with both hands.
Brace your core and squeeze the glutes.
Drive through the heels to lift the hips up.
Extend the hips to a straight line with the body.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top.
Lower the hips back down with control.
Strong glute builder
Easy at-home weighted move
Trains the hamstrings
Useful glute builder
No gym needed
Builds the posterior chain

description.en: The bottle weighted single leg romanian deadlift is performed standing on one leg while hinging forward and lowering water jugs or bottles toward the floor. It builds hamstring and glute strength and trains balance hard. It is a great home alternative to barbell RDLs.

en: Stand tall holding a weighted bottle in each hand.
Lift one leg slightly off the floor behind you.
Brace your core and keep a slight bend in the standing knee.
Hinge forward at the hip while extending the back leg behind you.
Keep the back leg in line with your torso.
Lower the bottles toward the floor along your standing leg.
Continue until you feel a stretch in the standing hamstring.
Drive your hips forward to return to standing. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Builds single-leg hamstring strength
Trains balance
No gym equipment required
Useful for home training
Easy to scale by bottle weight
Improves hip hinge pattern

description.en: The cable crossover is a single-joint chest isolation exercise performed on a dual cable machine. Standing between two pulleys, you bring the handles together in front of your body in a sweeping arc. Cables provide constant tension across the entire range of motion, making the cable crossover one of the most effective chest finishers for hypertrophy.

en: Set the cable pulleys at or slightly above shoulder height for a standard mid-chest crossover. Attach a single-grip handle to each pulley.

Grasp the handles with palms facing forward or down. Step forward with one foot in a staggered stance for stability and walk far enough away from the stack that there is constant tension on the cables in the start position.
Start with your arms out to the sides, slightly in front of your body, with a soft bend in your elbows.
Keeping that elbow bend locked in, bring your hands together in front of your chest in a sweeping arc, leading with your elbows.
Squeeze your chest hard at the bottom for a one-second peak contraction. Hands can meet, cross slightly, or stop just short depending on shoulder comfort.
Slowly return the handles to the start position under control, feeling a stretch across your chest. Do not let the weight stack slam down.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Set the pulleys low to bias the upper chest, or high to bias the lower chest.
Provides constant tension on the chest throughout the entire range of motion
Allows you to target the upper or lower chest by adjusting pulley height
Easier on the shoulders than dumbbell flys for many lifters
Excellent finishing exercise after compound chest pressing
Lets you train the chest without holding heavy free weights overhead

musclesWorked: Pectoralis major (upper, middle, and lower fibers depending on pulley height)

description.en: The cable half kneeling external rotation is a rotator cuff isolation move done from a half kneeling position. The lifter grips a cable with the elbow tucked at the side and externally rotates the forearm out to the side. The half kneeling stance braces the body for clean rotator work.

en: Set a cable to the lowest setting and attach a single handle.
Drop into a half kneeling position perpendicular to the cable.
Grip the handle with the outside hand.
Tuck the elbow tight against the side at 90 degrees.
Brace your core and keep the torso upright.
Externally rotate the forearm out to the side.
Squeeze the rotator cuff at the end range.
Rotate back to the start with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong rotator cuff builder
Trains shoulder health
Half kneeling stance braces the body
Useful pre-pressing move
Builds shoulder stability
Strong rehab move

description.en: The cable incline biceps curl is performed lying on an incline bench facing away from a low cable station. Holding a handle or bar attached to the cable, your arms hang behind your body in a fully stretched position. The incline angle plus cable tension creates strong constant resistance through the entire bicep range.

en: Set an incline bench facing away from a low cable station.
Attach a single handle or short bar to a low cable pulley.
Lie back on the incline bench with the cable behind you.
Grip the handle with an underhand grip and let your arm hang behind you.
Pin your shoulder back against the bench.
Curl the handle up by bending only at the elbow.
Continue until your forearm is roughly vertical.
Squeeze your bicep at the top, then lower with control to the stretched position.
Constant cable tension through the range
Strong stretch on the bicep at the bottom
Eliminates body english
Builds bicep size at the long head
Different stimulus than standard incline curls
Useful for hypertrophy training

description.en: The cable pulldown bicep curl is a hybrid exercise that combines a wide-grip lat pulldown with a bicep curl in one continuous movement. It is a time-efficient way to train both the back and biceps with a single setup, useful for finishers, supersets, or limited-time training.

en: Sit at a lat pulldown station with thighs locked under the pad. Grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands wider than shoulder-width.
Pull the bar down toward your upper chest in a strict lat pulldown.
At the bottom of the pulldown, hold the bar at chest level with elbows down.
Curl the bar up toward your face by bending only at the elbows. Keep elbows pinned to your sides.
At the top of the curl, slowly extend your arms back down to the chest position.
Then let the bar travel back up to the starting overhead position.
Repeat the combined pulldown-then-curl for the desired number of reps.
Use moderate weight — both muscle groups need to be challenged.
Combines back and bicep work in one movement
Time-efficient for full upper-body pulling
Useful as a finisher or for limited training time
Builds the lats and biceps simultaneously
Trains the muscles together as they function in sport
Easy to load and progress

description.en: The cable seated floor one arm concentration curl is a concentration curl variation using a low cable. The lifter sits on the floor and braces the elbow on the inner thigh, then curls the cable handle. The constant cable tension hammers the bicep peak.

en: Set a cable to the lowest setting with a single handle.
Sit on the floor in front of the cable stack.
Set the feet wide and bend the knees out.
Grip the handle with one hand and brace the elbow on the inner thigh.
Brace your core and lean slightly forward.
Curl the handle up toward the shoulder.
Squeeze the bicep hard at the top.
Lower back down with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong bicep peak builder
Constant cable tension
Trains unilateral biceps
Useful arm finisher
Strong cable move
Builds bicep size

description.en: The cable twisting overhead press is a unique compound exercise where you press a low-cable handle overhead while rotating your torso. The combination trains the shoulders, triceps, and rotational core simultaneously. It is excellent for athletes who need rotational power combined with overhead pressing strength.

en: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle.
Stand sideways to the cable, with the handle on your right side. Grip with your right hand at shoulder height.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core.
Press the handle up and overhead while rotating your torso to the left, away from the cable.
At lockout, your right arm is fully extended overhead and your torso has rotated significantly.
Reverse the motion — rotate back to start while lowering the handle to your shoulder.
Complete all reps on the right, then switch sides.
Use moderate weight — control through the rotation matters more than load.
Combines pressing with rotational power
Trains the shoulders, triceps, and obliques together
Develops athletic rotational strength
Carries over to throwing and striking sports
Constant cable tension
Builds core anti-rotation control

description.en: Camel Pose (Ustrasana) is a deep kneeling backbend yoga pose where you arch your spine backward and reach your hands to your heels. It deeply opens the chest, hip flexors, and quadriceps while strengthening the back. It is energizing and demands good spinal mobility.

en: Kneel on the floor with knees hip-width apart, tops of feet on the floor.
Place your hands on your lower back with fingers pointing down for support.
Lift your chest tall. Squeeze your glutes.
Slowly arch backward, leading with your chest. Keep your hips pushed forward over your knees.
If comfortable, reach back to grasp your heels with both hands.
Open your chest fully. Let your head drop back gently if your neck allows.
Hold for 5 to 8 breaths.
To exit, bring your hands back to your lower back, lift your chest, and rise to upright.
Deeply opens the chest, hips, and quads
Counteracts forward-hunched posture
Strengthens the back
Energizing and uplifting
Improves spinal extension mobility
No equipment needed

description.en: Climbing monkey bars is a fundamental bodyweight exercise where you traverse a series of overhead bars hand-over-hand. It builds grip strength, lat power, shoulder stability, and core engagement. It is one of the most fun and functional bodyweight exercises and a hallmark of natural movement training.

en: Reach up and grip the first monkey bar with both hands using an overhand or mixed grip.
Lift your feet off the ground. Hang from the bar with arms extended.
Engage your core and shoulders to keep your body stable — minimize swinging.
Reach forward with your right hand to grip the next bar.
Pull yourself forward as you transfer your weight to the right hand.
Reach with your left hand to grip the next bar.
Continue alternating hands, traversing the length of the bars.
Drop down at the end. Rest. Build up to multiple traverses or longer holds.
Builds elite grip strength and endurance
Develops lat strength and shoulder stability
Builds core engagement
Foundational bodyweight skill
Fun and functional
Used in obstacle course racing

description.en: The couch stretch is a deep hip flexor and quad stretch performed by kneeling with the back foot pressed against a couch, bench, or wall behind you. It is widely considered one of the most effective stretches for opening chronically tight hips from sitting. The position can be intense — work into it gradually.

en: Kneel facing away from a couch, bench, or wall.
Place your right shin vertically against the couch with the top of your right foot pressing against the surface.
Step your left foot forward into a 90-degree lunge position. Left foot flat on the floor.
Brace your core. Squeeze your right glute hard — this protects the lower back.
Push your hips forward gently. Feel the deep stretch through your right hip flexor and quad.
For more intensity, raise your torso to fully upright and reach your arms overhead.
For maximum intensity, gently arch your upper back.
Hold for 30 seconds to 2 minutes per side. Breathe deeply.
One of the deepest hip flexor and quad stretches available
Critical for anyone who sits a lot
Improves hip extension dramatically
Carries over to squat depth and running performance
Builds glute activation through the back-leg squeeze
Used heavily in mobility-focused programs

description.en: The dumbbell decline one arm fly performs the decline dumbbell fly one arm at a time. While one hand rests on the chest or down at the side, the working arm performs a strict fly motion with full range. Single-arm work corrects pec imbalances and adds an anti-rotation challenge to the core.

en: Set a bench to a decline angle and secure your feet on the foot pads.
Lie back with a single dumbbell in your right hand.
Press the dumbbell up over your chest with arm extended.
Place your left hand on your chest or at your side.
Maintain a slight bend in the working elbow.
Lower the dumbbell out to the side in a wide arc.
Continue until you feel a strong stretch in the chest.
Squeeze your chest to bring the dumbbell back over your chest. Switch arms.
Corrects pec imbalances
Strong unilateral chest isolation
Lower pec emphasis
Adds core anti-rotation challenge
Strong stretch on each rep
Useful for chest specialization

description.en: The dumbbell hammer grip incline bench two arm row is a chest supported row with a neutral grip. Pressing the chest into the incline bench removes lower back fatigue and isolates the lats and mid back.

en: Set an incline bench to about 30 to 45 degrees.
Grab two dumbbells and lie chest down on the bench.
Hold the dumbbells with a neutral hammer grip and arms hanging.
Brace the core and keep the chest pressed into the pad.
Pull both dumbbells up by driving the elbows back and up.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top of the row.
Lower the dumbbells slowly back to a full arm hang.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Isolates the lats and mid back with chest support.
Removes lower back load for safer high volume rowing.
Hammer grip is shoulder and elbow friendly.
Builds back thickness and pulling strength.
Trains both sides equally with a barbell free option.
Excellent assistance for deadlifts and pull ups.

description.en: The dumbbell lying one arm supinated triceps extension is a unilateral skullcrusher with a supinated palm up grip. The lifter lies on a bench and lowers the dumbbell to the opposite side shoulder. The supinated grip and cross body path target the triceps in a fresh way.

en: Lie on a flat bench holding a dumbbell in one hand.
Press the dumbbell up over the chest with palm facing up.
Set the upper arm vertical pointing at the ceiling.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Lower the dumbbell across to the opposite side shoulder.
Stop just before the dumbbell touches the shoulder.
Press back up to lockout extending the elbow.
Squeeze the tricep at the top. Switch sides.
Strong unilateral tricep builder
Unique angle
Trains the long head
Builds arm symmetry
Useful arm builder
Strong dumbbell move

description.en: The dumbbell one arm bench fly performs the flat bench dumbbell fly one arm at a time. While one hand rests on the chest or down at the side, the working arm performs a strict fly with full range. Single-arm work corrects pec imbalances and adds a strong anti-rotation challenge to the core.

en: Lie on a flat bench with a single dumbbell in your right hand.
Press the dumbbell up over your chest with arm extended.
Place your left hand on your chest or at your side.
Maintain a slight bend in the working elbow.
Lower the dumbbell out to the side in a wide arc.
Continue until you feel a strong stretch in the chest.
Squeeze your chest to bring the dumbbell back over your chest.
Complete reps on one side, then switch arms.
Corrects pec imbalances
Strong unilateral chest isolation
Adds core anti-rotation challenge
Strong stretch on each rep
Builds chest size
Useful for chest specialization

description.en: The dumbbell seated drag curl performs the drag curl pattern from a seated position. By dragging the dumbbells up along the body while keeping the elbows back, you isolate the long head of the biceps. The seated position eliminates body english entirely and forces strict form.

en: Sit on a bench with feet flat on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing forward.
Sit tall with chest up and shoulders back.
Brace your core and pull your elbows back behind your body.
Drag the dumbbells up along your sides, keeping them close to the body.
Continue curling until the dumbbells reach the upper ribs.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the dumbbells back down along the sides with control.
Isolates the long head of the biceps
Seated position eliminates body english
Strict form throughout
Builds bicep peak
Strong forearm engagement
Useful for breaking through bicep plateaus

description.en: The ez barbell standing wrist curl is a behind the back wrist curl using an ez bar. The lifter holds the bar behind the body at the hips with palms facing back, then curls the wrists. The behind the back position isolates the wrist flexors.

en: Stand tall with an ez curl bar behind the body at hip height.
Grip the bar with both hands palms facing back.
Set the elbows fully extended.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Allow the bar to roll down to the fingertips.
Curl the wrists up squeezing the forearms.
Lift the bar as high as the wrists allow.
Lower the bar back down with control.
Strong forearm builder
Trains the wrist flexors
Easy to overload
Builds grip strength
Useful arm builder
Strong ez bar move

description.en: The forearms stand yoga pose pincha mayurasana is an advanced inversion done balanced on the forearms. The legs lift overhead while the shoulders and core stabilize the inverted position. It builds serious shoulder strength and balance.

en: Kneel on the floor with the forearms placed shoulder width apart.
Press the palms flat with the elbows directly under the shoulders.
Walk the feet in toward the elbows.
Lift the hips high so the torso comes vertical.
Kick one leg up overhead to start the inversion.
Drive the second leg up to meet the first.
Squeeze the legs together and point the toes.
Hold balanced on the forearms then come down with control.
Builds serious shoulder and arm strength.
Improves balance and body awareness.
Stretches the spine in inversion.
Trains the core for stability.
Advanced inversion progression.

description.en: The half pigeon hip stretch (Eka Pada Rajakapotasana) is a deep yoga hip opener. The lifter sits with one leg bent in front and the other extended behind. The pose stretches the glutes of the front leg and the hip flexors of the back leg.

en: Start in a downward dog or table top position.
Bring one knee forward toward the wrist of the same side.
Set the bent knee on the floor with the shin angled forward.
Extend the back leg straight behind with the top of the foot on the floor.
Square the hips toward the floor.
Lower the torso forward over the front leg.
Hold the stretch with steady breath.
Walk back to the start. Switch legs and repeat.
Deep glute stretch
Stretches the hip flexors
Strong yoga hip opener
Builds hip mobility
Useful cool down move
Easy to do anywhere

description.en: The half-seated leg circle is a hip mobility and core exercise where you sit with hands behind you for support, lift one leg, and draw circles in the air. It builds hip flexor strength, hip mobility, and lower-ab control.

en: Sit on the floor. Lean back slightly with hands behind you for support.
Extend your right leg straight in front of you, lifted a few inches off the floor.
Draw circles with your right foot — clockwise for the desired reps, then counterclockwise.
Keep the circles controlled and smooth.
Your left foot stays flat on the floor for stability.
Complete circles in both directions, then switch legs.
Keep your core braced throughout.
Aim for 8 to 10 circles per direction per leg.
Builds hip flexor strength and control
Improves hip mobility
Develops lower ab stability
No equipment needed
Useful warm-up or rehab exercise
Builds hip joint awareness

description.en: The inverted wide row is a wide-grip variation of the inverted row, performed underneath a low bar. The wider grip shifts emphasis to the upper back, rhomboids, and rear delts compared to the standard shoulder-width grip. It is a strong choice for upper back development with bodyweight only.

en: Set a barbell in a power rack at about waist height.
Lie on the floor underneath the bar.
Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width, palms facing away.
Position your body in a straight line with heels on the floor.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Pull your chest up to the bar by leading with the elbows out wide.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together hard at the top.
Lower yourself back down with control to a full hang.
Wide grip emphasizes upper back
Strong rear delt and rhomboid engagement
Builds back strength with bodyweight
No weights required
Different stimulus than standard inverted row
Useful for posture work

description.en: The kettlebell backward lunge (reverse lunge) is performed holding kettlebells at your sides or in the front rack while stepping backward into a lunge. Stepping backward is generally easier on the knees and maintains more tension on the front leg throughout.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a KB in each hand at your sides (or in the front rack).
Step your right foot back two to three feet behind you.
Lower your right knee toward the floor by bending both knees.
Descend until your right knee is just above the floor.
Drive through your front (left) foot to return to standing.
Alternate legs or complete all reps on one side.
Keep your torso upright.
Aim for 8 to 12 reps per leg.
Easier on the knees than forward lunges
Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally
KB handles demand grip engagement
Easy to scale by adjusting weight
Exposes left-right imbalances
Useful at-home leg exercise

description.en: Ladder drills are agility exercises performed by moving through an agility ladder laid on the ground, stepping in and out of the ladder squares with various footwork patterns. They build foot speed, coordination, balance, and cardiovascular conditioning. They are a standard training tool in virtually every sport.

en: Lay an agility ladder flat on the ground. Stand at one end facing the length of the ladder.
Choose a footwork pattern (e.g., two-feet-in-each-box, single-foot-per-box, in-in-out-out, ickey shuffle).
Begin moving through the ladder, placing your feet precisely in each square.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Keep your arms pumping for speed and balance.
Move as fast as you can while maintaining clean, precise footwork.
Walk back to the start and repeat with the same or a different pattern.
Perform 4 to 8 passes through the ladder per drill.
Quality of footwork matters more than raw speed — get the pattern clean, then speed up.
Builds foot speed and agility
Improves coordination and neuromuscular control
Develops fast-twitch muscle fibers
Excellent sport-specific warm-up
Fun and engaging training tool
Builds cardiovascular conditioning

description.en: The lying leg tuck hip stretch with overhead hands is a supine stretch that combines a knee tuck with an overhead arm reach. The reach lengthens the side body while the tuck stretches the glute and lower back.

en: Lie on the back with the legs extended.
Bend one knee and bring it toward the chest.
Hold the shin with the same side hand.
Reach the opposite arm overhead along the floor.
Brace the core and keep the shoulders flat.
Pull the knee deep into the chest.
Feel the stretch through the side body and glute.
Hold for the desired duration then switch sides.
Stretches the glute.
Lengthens the side body.
Decompresses the lumbar spine.
Useful for hip mobility.
Joint friendly stretch.

description.en: The pelvic tilt into bridge is a Pilates-style mobility exercise that combines a posterior pelvic tilt with a sequential roll into a glute bridge. It teaches segmental spinal articulation, builds glute activation, and improves lumbar control. It is a foundational warm-up exercise for spine and glute health.

en: Lie flat on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Begin with a posterior pelvic tilt: press your lower back firmly into the floor and tilt your pelvis up toward your ribs.
From the pelvic tilt, sequentially roll your spine off the floor — tailbone, lower back, mid-back — until you reach a glute bridge position.
At the top, your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze your glutes.
Reverse the motion: roll your spine back down sequentially — mid-back, lower back, tailbone.
End with the posterior pelvic tilt before releasing.
Move slowly and with control. Each vertebra should leave and return to the floor sequentially.
Repeat for 8 to 12 reps as a warm-up or core activation.
Teaches segmental spinal articulation
Builds glute activation
Improves lumbar control
Excellent warm-up for lower-body training
Useful for rehabilitation and posture work
No equipment needed

description.en: Puppy Pose (Uttana Shishosana) is a gentle yoga stretch performed from a tabletop position by walking your hands forward and lowering your chest toward the floor while keeping your hips directly above your knees. It deeply stretches the chest, shoulders, and spine — like a combination of Child's Pose and Downward Dog.

en: Start in a tabletop position on your hands and knees. Hips directly above knees, shoulders above wrists.
Walk your hands forward as far as you can while keeping your hips stacked above your knees.
Lower your chest toward the floor. Let your forehead or chin rest on the mat.
Keep your arms active — press your palms into the floor and reach forward.
Feel the stretch through your chest, shoulders, armpits, and upper back.
Keep your hips high — directly above your knees. Do not let them drift forward.
Hold for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe deeply into the stretch.
To release, walk your hands back toward your knees.
Deeply stretches the chest, shoulders, and upper back
Opens the armpits and lats
Extends the spine gently
More active than Child’s Pose, deeper than Downward Dog
Calming and restorative
No equipment needed

description.en: The push up hand by hand is a push up variation that walks the hands. The lifter performs a push up, then moves one hand forward and the other to match before the next rep. The walking pattern adds coordination and core demand to the push up.

en: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core hard.
Perform a standard push up lowering and pressing back up.
At the top move one hand forward.
Move the other hand forward to match.
Perform another push up.
Continue alternating push ups with hand walks forward.
Combo chest and core builder
Trains coordination
Builds shoulder stability
No equipment needed
Useful core builder
Strong push up variation

description.en: The resistance band seated straight back row is a strict seated row using a resistance band. The lifter sits with legs extended and the band anchored low in front, then rows the band to the body. The strict straight back form keeps the focus on the back muscles.

en: Anchor a resistance band low in front of you.
Sit on the floor with legs extended.
Loop the band around the feet or grip the handles.
Set the back tall and slightly leaned forward.
Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades.
Pull the band toward the body driving the elbows back.
Squeeze the upper back at the end of the row.
Lower with control to the start.
Strong back builder
No machine needed
Trains the lats
Builds back thickness
Useful at-home back move
Strong band move

description.en: The reverse dip performs dips with a straight bar behind your back — similar to Korean dips. You face away from the bar, grip it behind you, and dip. It places extreme demand on shoulder extension and the chest.

en: Stand in front of a bar at hip height, facing away. Grip behind you.
Support your weight on the bar behind you. Feet forward.
Lower by bending elbows — the bar is behind your body.
Lower until elbows reach about 90 degrees or you feel a deep chest stretch.
Press back up.
Requires good shoulder extension mobility.
Start with small range and progress.
Aim for 5 to 10 reps.
Extreme chest stretch from behind-body position
Builds shoulder extension strength
Advanced bodyweight pressing variation
Different stimulus from standard dips
Develops shoulder mobility under load
Impressive calisthenics skill

description.en: The lever seated calf press is a calf exercise performed on a seated leg press machine. With your legs nearly extended, you press the platform up and down using only your calves by pointing and flexing your toes. The machine allows heavy calf loading with a full range of motion from deep stretch to peak contraction.

en: Sit on the seated leg press machine. Press the platform out until your legs are nearly fully extended (slight bend in knees).
Slide your feet down so only the balls of your feet and toes are on the bottom edge of the platform. Your heels should hang off the platform.
Release the safety handles. Brace your core.
Let your toes pull back toward your shins to drop into a deep calf stretch.
Press through the balls of your feet to push the platform by pointing your toes. Rise as high as possible.
Squeeze your calves hard at the top for one second.
Lower under control back to the deep stretch. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Use moderate weight and aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Allows heavy calf loading with full range of motion
Deep stretch at the bottom and peak contraction at the top
Easy to load progressively
Reduces balance demand vs standing calf raises
Useful when no dedicated calf machine is available
Targets the gastrocnemius with nearly straight legs

description.en: The side crunch II is a variation of the classic side crunch performed lying on the floor. The setup includes a different leg or hand position to slightly change the angle of pull on the obliques. The result is a focused oblique isolation that supplements the standard side crunch.

en: Lie on your back on the floor.
Bend both knees with feet flat on the floor.
Drop both knees together to your right side.
Place your hands behind your head with elbows wide.
Brace your abs hard.
Crunch your left obliques by lifting your shoulders off the floor.
Lift the left shoulder higher than the right toward the ceiling.
Squeeze the obliques at the top, then lower with control. Switch sides after the set.
Direct oblique isolation
No equipment required
Builds oblique strength
Easy to scale by adjusting range
Useful for oblique specialization
Strong mind-muscle connection

description.en: The smith incline reverse grip press combines the incline angle with a reverse (underhand) grip. Research shows this combination produces the highest activation of the upper chest fibers of any pressing variation. The smith machine guides the bar path so you can focus on chest contraction.

en: Set an incline bench inside a smith machine.
Lie back with the bar over your upper chest.
Grip the bar with an underhand grip at shoulder width.
Unrack the bar and brace your core.
Lower the bar to your upper chest with control.
Keep your elbows tucked toward your sides.
Press the bar back up to the start.
Lock out at the top before the next rep.
Maximally targets the upper chest
Stable smith machine path
Reverse grip recruits triceps
Reduces shoulder strain
Easy to load progressively
Best move for upper chest activation

description.en: The smith one leg floor calf raise is a unilateral calf raise performed with a smith machine bar on the shoulders. The lifter rises onto the toes of one foot at a time from a flat floor. The smith bar adds load while the single leg work isolates each calf.

en: Set a smith machine bar at upper chest height.
Step under the bar and place it on the upper back.
Unrack the bar and step out.
Lift one foot up off the floor.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Rise onto the ball of the foot of the working leg.
Squeeze the calf hard at the top.
Lower the heel back down with control. Complete reps and switch legs.
Strong unilateral calf builder
Heavy load capacity
Builds calf size
Useful calf builder
Strong machine move
Trains balance

description.en: The Smith machine upright row is a trap and lateral-delt exercise performed using the Smith machine. The fixed bar path provides stability while you pull the bar up the front of your body. Use a wider grip and stop at chest height to keep the movement shoulder-friendly.

en: Stand inside the Smith machine. Position the bar at hip height.
Grip the bar with hands shoulder-width or slightly wider apart, overhand grip.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core.
Pull the bar straight up the front of your body by driving your elbows up and out.
Continue pulling until the bar reaches chest height. Do not pull higher.
Squeeze your traps and lateral delts at the top.
Lower the bar slowly under control to the starting position.
Use moderate weight. Use a wider grip to reduce shoulder impingement risk.
Stable bar path allows focus on the muscles
Builds the traps and lateral delts
Easier to control than free-weight versions
Useful for high-rep work
Wide grip reduces shoulder risk
Easy to load progressively

description.en: The Smith wide grip decline bench press combines three chest-focused techniques in one. The decline angle hits the lower pec, the wide grip emphasizes the outer chest, and the Smith machine fixed path eliminates balance demands. The combination is a strong outer-lower chest specialization variation.

en: Set a decline bench under the Smith machine bar.
Lie back with feet secured on the foot pads, eyes under the bar.
Grip the bar wider than your normal bench press grip.
Pull your shoulder blades back into the bench.
Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists.
Lower the bar with control to your lower chest.
Press the bar back up to lockout, squeezing your chest.
Re-rack the bar by rotating your wrists when finished.
Targets outer lower chest fibers
Fixed bar path removes balance demands
Allows focus on chest contraction
Useful for chest specialization
Heavier loading possible than free bar for many lifters
Builds chest size and lower pec definition

description.en: The standing ab twist is a simple core exercise where you stand with feet shoulder-width apart and rotate your torso side to side, often with arms extended forward or holding a weight. It builds oblique strength and rotational control while standing — useful for athletes who need standing core strength.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Bend your knees slightly.
Extend both arms forward at chest height with palms together (or hold a light weight).
Brace your core. Pull your shoulders back.
Rotate your torso to the right as far as comfortable. Keep your hips facing forward.
Pause briefly at the end of the rotation.
Rotate back through center and continue to the left.
Continue alternating side to side rhythmically.
Keep the rotation in your thoracic spine — not your lumbar spine.
Builds oblique strength
Trains rotational control
Warms up the thoracic spine
Useful for athletes
No equipment needed
Quick and accessible

description.en: The standing T-raise is a shoulder activation and postural exercise where you lift both arms straight out to the sides at shoulder height (forming a T shape) with thumbs pointing up. It activates the rear deltoids, middle trapezius, and rhomboids — key muscles for posture and shoulder health.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Arms at your sides, thumbs pointing forward.
Brace your core. Pull your shoulders back and down.
Lift both arms straight out to the sides until they are at shoulder height, forming a T shape.
Keep your thumbs pointing upward. Squeeze your shoulder blades together.
Hold for one to two seconds at the top.
Lower under control back to your sides.
Repeat for 10 to 15 reps. Use no weight or very light dumbbells.
This is an activation exercise — do not go heavy.
Activates the rear delts and mid-traps
Builds postural muscles
Excellent warm-up before pressing or rowing
Improves shoulder positioning and scapular control
No equipment needed
Useful for rehabilitation and posture correction

description.en: The strongman tire flip is a classic strongman exercise where you flip a heavy tractor tire end-over-end. It combines a deadlift-style initial lift with an explosive hip drive and pushing finish. It builds full-body explosive power and is one of the most iconic strongman exercises.

en: Stand in front of a heavy tractor tire. Feet shoulder-width apart, close to the tire.
Squat down and grip the bottom of the tire with both hands, fingers underneath.
Drive through your legs to lift the tire, like a deadlift. Keep your back flat.
As the tire reaches hip height, drive your hips into the tire and push it forward.
Transition from pulling to pushing — switch your hands from under the tire to pushing on it.
Push the tire over and let it slam down.
Walk to the other side and repeat.
Use proper lifting mechanics. Never round your back during the initial pull.
Builds explosive full-body power
Combines pulling, hip drive, and pushing
Iconic strongman exercise
Excellent conditioning
Develops mental toughness
Full-body movement

description.en: The suspender handstand push-up places the feet in the foot cradles of a suspension trainer in front of a wall. The body then performs a handstand push-up with feet supported. The setup is more accessible than a free-standing HSPU and excellent for shoulder strength.

en: Set the suspension trainer in front of a wall at low height.
Place your feet in the foot cradles facing away from the wall.
Walk your hands out into a handstand push-up position with feet up high.
Position your hands wider than shoulder-width.
Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line.
Bend your elbows to lower your head toward the floor.
Stop just before your head touches.
Press through your hands to drive back up to full lockout.
Builds elite shoulder strength
Trains overhead pressing
Builds core stability
No wall scrape needed
Advanced bodyweight move
Strong handstand progression

description.en: The twist step stretch combines a step into a lunge position with a torso twist toward the front leg. The lunge opens the hip flexor of the back leg while the twist mobilizes the thoracic spine. It is an effective dynamic stretch used in athletic warm-ups.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Step forward with one leg into a deep lunge.
Place the same-side hand on the floor inside the front foot.
Brace your core and keep your back leg straight.
Reach the opposite arm up and rotate your torso toward the front leg.
Look up at your reaching hand.
Hold briefly at the top of the rotation.
Return your hands to the floor and step back to standing. Switch sides.
Opens the hip flexors
Mobilizes the thoracic spine
Useful as a dynamic warm-up
Combines hip and spine work
Improves rotational mobility

description.en: The V sit toe tap is a V sit variation that adds toe taps for coordination. The lifter holds a V sit and reaches across to tap the opposite toe. It is a strong core and hip flexor builder.

en: Sit on the floor with the legs straight in front.
Lean back and lift the legs into a V sit.
Set the body in a V shape with abs engaged.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Reach one hand across to tap the opposite toe.
Return to the V sit position.
Tap the other toe with the opposite hand.
Continue alternating sides.
Loads the core
Trains the obliques
Strong V sit variation
Builds the hip flexors
Useful core move

description.en: The weighted plate standing around the world is a shoulder and core endurance drill. Holding a plate at arms length and circling it around the head loads the delts isometrically while the core resists the shifting weight.

en: Stand tall with the feet shoulder width apart.
Hold a weight plate with both hands at chest level.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Press the plate forward with the arms extended.
Circle the plate around the head from front to side.
Continue circling around behind the head and back to the start.
Keep the arms straight throughout.
Reverse direction and continue for the working set.
Trains the shoulders.
Loads the core for stability.
Builds shoulder endurance.
Useful conditioning drill.
Improves spatial control.

description.en: The weighted seated one arm reverse wrist curl is a forearm extensor isolation move. Sitting on a bench with the forearm braced and a dumbbell in a pronated grip targets the often neglected back of the forearm.

en: Sit on a bench with feet flat on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell with one hand using a pronated grip.
Rest the forearm on your thigh with the wrist hanging off the knee.
Let the dumbbell hang down with the wrist fully flexed.
Brace the core and stabilize the forearm with the free hand if needed.
Curl the back of the hand up by extending the wrist.
Squeeze the forearm extensors at the top.
Lower the dumbbell slowly back to full wrist flexion and complete all reps then switch.
Isolates the forearm extensors often missed in standard curls.
Builds wrist and forearm strength balance.
Improves grip and gripping endurance.
Single arm focus exposes imbalances.
Joint friendly with controlled tempo.
Carryover to compound lifts and grip sports.

description.en: The weighted straight bar dip is a dip variation performed on a single straight bar. The lifter holds the bar in front of the hips with both hands and dips down with the bar against the body. The single bar forces a slight forward lean that hits the chest hard.

en: Hook a dip belt with weight around the waist or wear a weighted vest.
Grip a single straight bar with both hands at hip width.
Press up to lockout with the bar in front of the body.
Brace your core and lean slightly forward.
Lower the body by bending the elbows.
Allow the bar to slide up the body slightly as you descend.
Lower until the upper arms are parallel to the floor.
Press back up to lockout squeezing the triceps and chest.
Strong tricep and chest builder
Adds weight to dips
Unique single bar angle
Builds upper body size
Useful tricep builder
Strong compound move
